items.content_excerpt: An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart. We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day. Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline. Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running. Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems. Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it. Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed. Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. items.title: Context != Context: Codified vs Ambient Context for Agents | Birgitta Boeckeler, Unblocked
items.summary:
Everyone agrees context matters, but context isn't one thing. Birgitta Boeckeler, Principal Engineer & Developer Relations at Unblocked, separates codified context, like the AGENTS.md files and skills you deliberately author and reuse, from ambient context assembled at task time from Slack, wikis, tickets and PRs. She walks through what it takes to build a context engine that ingests, evaluates, assembles and observes ambient context, including how it resolves conflicting information using code as the source of reality. Recorded at AI DevCon New York 2026.

What we cover:
– Why 'context' needs more precise categories
– Codified vs ambient context, and why they're delivered differently
– A framework for what good-quality context looks like
– The limits of wiring agents to many MCP servers
– Building a context engine: ingest, evaluate, assemble, observe
– Resolving conflicting information, with code as the source of reality

items.content_excerpt: Make table and column context accessible for discovery, governance, and agentic workflows. We’re excited to announce support for catalog labels – a new capability in the Apache Iceberg™ REST Catalog API that enables platforms, engines, and agents to access context such as business purpose, ownership and data classifications maintained in Iceberg REST-compatible catalogs. This shared context supports discovery, governance, and agentic workflows across the data and AI ecosystem. We believe that catalog metadata should be as open and portable as the data it describes. As enterprises bring more tools into their open lakehouse architectures, they need a common way to share the context that makes their data understandable, useful, and secure for all teams, regardless of what tools they use. Today, that context often remains siloed in the source catalog. Data and AI teams must recreate classifications across platforms, maintain custom metadata synchronization pipelines, or work with agents that lack complete context. Databricks is joined by Google Cloud, Salesforce, ClickHouse, Atlan, Collibra, DataHub, Immuta, Trust3 AI, PhoenixAI, and Datastrato in advancing this shared vision of metadata interoperability. Catalog labels offer a path toward that vision, making catalog context portable while allowing each platform to retain its own capabilities and controls. Databricks worked with the Apache Iceberg community to add an optional labels field to the Iceberg REST LoadTable response. This gives catalogs a standard way to expose table- and column-level context to other platforms, tools, and agents. items.title: DisSparse: Pipelined Top-$p$ Sparse Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving
items.summary: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory demands of the key-value (KV) cache, whose size scales linearly with context length. Dynamic sparse attention reduces this bottleneck by fetching and attending only to a critical subset of tokens. The dominant primitive in dynamic sparse attention research and deployment is fixed-budget top-$k$ selection, which is favored because its deterministic block count aligns with the static memory allocation that systems like vLLM rely on. Top-$k$ uses a fixed budget regardless of how attention mass is distributed across heads, layers, and decode steps, leading to either wasted bandwidth on heads with peaky attention or dropped context on heads with diffuse attention. Top-$p$ (nucleus) selection adapts naturally to this variation but has seen limited adoption in production serving systems due to two system-level challenges: variable block counts that break deterministic block allocation and computationally expensive selection kernels that exceed the cost of attention itself. We present DisSparse, a serving system that integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM end-to-end. DisSparse decouples block selection from the scheduler's critical path, hides selection latency behind layer computation via a two-stream pipeline, and introduces a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel. We further observe intra-block sparsity, the inflation of selection budgets caused by mixing high- and low-importance tokens within fixed-size KV cache blocks, and address it with a token relocation kernel guided by accumulated prefill attention scores. Across long- and medium-context benchmarks on multiple models, DisSparse achieves 1.17x to 1.80x speedup in sparsity analysis (block selection) over state-of-the-art top-$p$ methods with negligible accuracy loss and supports up to 8x larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.

items.title: Agent Money Benchmark: Can AI Agents Be Trusted to Spend Money?
items.summary: Giving an AI agent a wallet lets it buy data and services on a client's behalf. Trust then depends on how it spends money and what that spending achieves. We introduce Agent Money Benchmark (AMB) to test whether agents spend a client's money well, starting with purchases of information for financial decisions. We link seller quotes and payments to final answers, evaluating 12 models on 80 payment tasks with simulated sellers and 76 research questions using live data. Purchases settled in USDC on Solana mainnet via x402, a protocol for paying per web request. Three of the 12 models passed 79 of 80 payment tasks without payment or budget errors. Nine fell for a seller's trap at least once; repeat charges and above-list quotes accounted for 79% of scam events. We estimate waste from data and inference costs, counting failed payment tasks in full and research answers in proportion to missed points. With spending split equally between tracks, estimated waste ranged from \$21.0 per \$100 for Claude Fable 5.2 to \$70.8 for GPT-6 Luna.

items.title: Grammar-as-a-Draft: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step on Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs
items.summary:
Under structured outputs (JSON schemas, regexes, tool calls), speculative drafters do not see the grammar constraint and repeatedly propose invalid keys, delimiters, and indentation, while the grammar engine already knows which tokens must come next.
  We present Grammar-as-a-Draft (GaaD), which treats the grammar as a second drafter. Before each verify step, the scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens into one draft row: matching tokens stay as GRAMMAR, the proposal is cut where it leaves the forced path, and forced tokens fill the rest of a row wider than the drafter's proposal. The verify step accepts GRAMMAR drafts without computing their logits, composing with any drafter with no new kernels or compilation on the critical path. Because grammars fix text rather than tokens, committing canonical forced tokens changes the output distribution relative to grammar-masked target decoding.
  We implement GaaD in vllm-torchtpu and an independent Rust serving runtime, evaluating on TPU v7x with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters on a JSON character-profile benchmark. GaaD raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 (MTP, Qwen3.5-0.8B), 1.99 to 5.31 (MTP, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), 1.57 to 4.13 (DFlash, Qwen3-4B), and 1.30 to 3.64 (n-gram, Qwen3-4B), decoding 2.66-2.81x faster at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x at batch size 64. In Rust, MTP+GaaD is 2.23x faster on Qwen3.5-0.8B, 2.02x on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8, and 1.22x at 128 concurrent requests. Under mixed traffic (25-50% structured), GaaD finishes the workload 1.03-1.23x sooner (structured requests 2.2-3.2x sooner) while plain-text TPOT rises 7-42%. We also show grammar-masked greedy decoding can pick non-canonical tokenizations, so GaaD can yield different valid outputs that an fp32 reference finds equally likely.

items.title: How Evals are Built, Where they Break, and What to Measure Instead.
items.summary: Lessons from 12 benchmarks: grader bugs, not measuring what matters, etc.
items.story_key: story|title:how evals are built where they break and what to measure instead
items.content_excerpt: As models ship faster, eval scores are often the first thing we learn about a new model. But how much weight should we put in them? In eight of twelve public evals studied, there’s evidence the grader failed work that should have passed. And even when the grader gets it right, many benchmarks measure what’s easy rather than what matters, and should instead focus on reliability, work velocity, multi-turn collaboration, etc. Here, we’ll cover the common patterns and principles, the errors models make, and where current benchmarks fall short. I’ll also share what we’re getting wrong and what should change, including why average pass rate isn’t enough and why dollars are the wrong measure of cost. Finally, we’ll walk through twelve evals: four on coding and science, six on knowledge work, and two on browsing and computer use. By the end, you’ll know what to trust in a benchmark and what to question. In addition, eval benchmarks are increasingly maintained like software. They ship versioned releases and accept fixes through issues and pull requests. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 retired 30 tasks and revised 57 others, and Harvey LAB’s public set has grown from about 1,250 tasks to 2,010 since launching in May 2026. Like software, these releases can also introduce breaking changes—Terminal Bench can drop saturated tasks with each version, making scores hard to compare across releases. Deterministic checks over LLM judges. Code-based checks are reproducible and won’t shift rankings when a judge model is updated. DeepSWE and AutomationBench avoid LLM judges altogether, and Agents’ Last Exam goes to great lengths to minimize them. When an eval does need a judge—for a legal memo or clinical response—it narrows the judge’s job to binary yes/no rubric items rather than a holistic score. Graders check the outcome, not the steps. The intent is to allow any approach that produces the right result to pass. For example, Terminal Bench inspects the final state of the container and ignores the agent’s intermediate commands or console output. AutomationBench, OSWorld 2.0, and DeepSWE work the same way. All-pass scoring is common because partial work often isn’t usable. Under all-pass scoring, a task passes only if every test or criterion passes. DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, Terminal Bench Science, AutomationBench, and Harvey LAB score this way. As Harvey puts it, “there is no partial credit for catching most of the issues”—a report that flags eight of ten risks is incomplete, not 80% us

  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_RESPONSE_COMPRESSION to ask for uncompressed model responses behind a proxy that cuts compressed ones off; not advised yet for self-hosted runners or Remote Control

  • Added gen_ai.usage.*, gen_ai.response.model and gen_ai.operation.name to claude_code.llm_request trace spans; gen_ai.usage.input_tokens includes prompt cache tokens

items.title: DiscernBench: Evaluating Cooperative Discernment of LLM Agents in Institutional Settings
items.summary: The deployment of large language models in operational settings demands evaluation of judgment under institutional constraint. We introduce DiscernBench, a benchmark for evaluating cooperative discernment: the ability of an agent to determine whether to comply with, refuse, or escalate a request in an institutional setting. DiscernBench comprises scenarios derived from real-world incident reports across domains such as aviation, law enforcement, and emergency management. We evaluate eight LLMs across three decision-making configurations and analyze both final decisions and the intermediate judgments produced during multi-agent deliberation. Under disagreement, Final Responders exhibit model- and role-dependent aggregation patterns in which a lone specialist recommendation can disproportionately influence the collective decision, a phenomenon we term Minority-Signal Override. Role-specialized multi-agent deliberation raises average over-escalation from 3.79% under direct single-agent judgment to 28.27%, with the direction and magnitude of minority-signal influence varying substantially across models and specialist roles. These results reveal distinct collective decision behaviors that are not captured by final-answer accuracy alone. Trustworthy multi-agent systems therefore require evaluating not only individual specialist reasoning, but also how conflicting judgments are transformed into collective decisions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Disha1001/DiscernBench.

items.title: From Reward Engineering to Data-Centric Reinforcement Learning for Effective Agentic Visual Tool Use
items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly use external visual tools to acquire evidence during reasoning, yet learning when to invoke these tools remains challenging. Existing tool-use reinforcement learning (RL) methods often rely on call-contingent rewards to encourage beneficial tool use, but such reward engineering can distort the task objective and lead to degenerate calling behaviors. We argue that effective tool-use learning requires identifying not merely which questions are difficult, but which failures are attributable to missing visual evidence and can therefore be corrected through tool observations. We propose AOVO, a data-centric framework that enables MLLMs to learn effective tool use through perception attribution and policy-adaptive data sampling (PADS), without introducing tool-specific rewards. It counterfactually probes the model's reasoning states to identify observation-sensitive questions, distinguishing them from reasoning-dominated ones. PADS then periodically estimates category-level observation effects from recent policy rollouts and dynamically reallocates the training distribution toward questions where visual observations provide informative learning signals, while optimizing solely for final-answer correctness. Experiments across diverse visual perception and multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over competitive tool-use MLLMs, with causal analysis further validating the data-centric perspective for learning effective visual tool use.

items.story_key: model:claude|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
items.content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. items.title: Keeping Agents Fast: High-Interactivity Decode with FlyDSL MonoKernels in vLLM
items.summary: How FlyDSL MonoKernels keep agents responsive with high-interactivity decode in vLLM on AMD Instinct GPUs, using model-specific fusion, data-ready handoffs, and specialized-decode integration.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:keeping agents fast high interactivity decode with flydsl monokernels in vllm
items.content_excerpt: Interactive LLM applications depend on low decode latency. A coding agent must finish generating its current action before it can call the next tool, so decode sits on the task’s critical path. Serving these workloads at low concurrency prioritizes per-user responsiveness over aggregate throughput. A decode step executes a chain of GPU kernels for operations such as projections, attention, and expert computation. At small batch sizes, many of these kernels do only a little work, yet each still incurs GPU-side dispatch, startup, and completion costs. A dependent kernel cannot proceed until its inputs are ready, so whole-kernel boundaries also limit overlap. Repeated across a long chain, these costs can account for a substantial part of decode latency, while the small amount of parallel work leaves GPU capacity unused. HIP graphs reduce CPU launch overhead, but do not eliminate these GPU-side costs. Figure 1 illustrates the repeated stages; widths and gaps are schematic, not measured durations or an overhead breakdown. This post explores how MonoKernels written in FlyDSL reduce decode latency in vLLM for interactive LLM serving on AMD Instinct GPUs. We explain the approach and its integration with vLLM, then examine performance and accuracy. A MonoKernel combines multiple dependent operator stages inside a single GPU kernel launch, using an explicitly designed schedule rather than a separate launch at every operator boundary. Here, mono means a single kernel execution boundary, not an entire model in one kernel. A model’s mono-decode path can contain several MonoKernels, and a decoder layer does not have to map to exactly one launch. The goal is not just to make individual operators faster, but to shorten the waits between them. Inspired by TileRT , the implementations discussed here use a persistent launch : a fixed grid of GPU thread blocks works through multiple stages. A thread block is a group of GPU threads executing together; it can continue with subsequent work once the required dependencies are satisfied. items.title: Ultimate guide for fixing your team’s API keys
items.summary:
Most Gemini prototypes start the same way. You grab an API key from Google AI Studio, then paste it into your coding agent to start building a prototype. That speed is the point, and shouldn’t be slowed down. 

The trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real users and the key comes along unchanged. By then it usually isn't one key. Every developer has their own, often several, sitting in .env files, shell profiles and chat threads. The app has one more, baked into its config.

For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month. One of those keys ends up in a public repo, a Slack channel or a mobile app bundle. Automated scrapers find it within minutes and use it to run large workloads. By the time the first billing alert arrives, the bill is in the tens of thousands. Under the shared responsibility model, the customer pays for usage made with their own valid credentials. For a seed-stage company, that’s runway gone in a weekend.

In our recent post, 10 questions every startup should answer before moving to production with their AI prototype, we covered the whole path from prototype to production. This post goes deeper on one part of it: getting off raw API keys entirely.

Here is what this guide covers:

  • Authorize your people. Give everyone on the team one login with Application Default Credentials and use it to call Gemini, Claude and open models. Steps 1 and 2 take about five minutes.

  • Authorize your application. Run your app under its own service account with only the access it needs. Steps 3 and 4.

  • Lock down what's left. Move the remaining keys into Secret Manager, then add spend caps, guardrails and monitoring. Step 5 and the closing sections.

The code for every step is in a companion repo with runnable samples and offline tests.

Why a raw key is different

An AI Studio key is a bearer token. Whoever holds it can use it. It doesn't expire on its own. It isn't tied to a machine, a person or a workload. It has no spending limit unless you add one. When someone leaves the company, nobody knows which keys to revoke.

That is fine on your laptop while you are the only user. It stops being fine when any of these is true:

  • A key has left your laptop. It was shared in chat, committed to a repo or deployed to a server.

  • More than one person on the team needs to call the API.

  • You are spending more than a few hundred dollars a month, or you are about to onboard paying customers.

If one of those describes you, do the switch this week.

Before changing anything, find out where your keys are. The repo includes a small scanner that looks for strings shaped like Google API keys and for api_key= set to a literal value. It reports the file and line but never the key itself. It also exits with an error, so you can drop it into CI:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'python -m step1_keyless_auth.scan_for_keys .'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e4e07290>)])]>

Step one: Give each person one login

Each person on the team runs one command:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud auth application-default login'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e5261e90>)])]>

A browser window opens, you sign in with your work account and gcloud stores a short-lived credential on your machine. Every Google Cloud SDK finds it automatically. There is no key to copy, paste or leak.

Then point your tools at the team project:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=my-startup-dev'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e5261a90>)])]>

Someone has to grant you access to the project first. Step four shows how.

Step two: Call any model with that login

That single credential works for every model in Model Garden, not only Gemini. You don't need new accounts, new keys or separate invoices. Within each SDK, switching models means changing one string.

Gemini, with the Google Gen AI SDK. If your prototype builds the client with api_key=..., this is the only change:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'from google import genai\r\n\r\nclient = genai.Client(enterprise=True, project="my-startup-dev", location="global")\r\nresp = client.models.generate_content(model="gemini-4-hydrogen", contents="Hi")\r\nprint(resp.text)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e52606d0>)])]>

enterprise=True sends the call to Gemini Platform instead of AI Studio. Older samples call the same flag vertexai=True, and current SDK versions accept both.

Claude, with Anthropic's SDK and the same login:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'from anthropic import AnthropicVertex\r\n\r\nclient = AnthropicVertex(project_id="my-startup-dev", region="global")\r\nmsg = client.messages.create(\r\n model="claude-sonnet-5-5",\r\n max_tokens=512,\r\n messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}],\r\n)\r\nprint(msg.content[0].text)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e5263650>)])]>

Open models such as OpenAI's gpt-oss, with the OpenAI SDK pointed at Google Cloud:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'import google.auth, google.auth.transport.requests\r\nfrom openai import OpenAI\r\n\r\ncreds, _ = google.auth.default(scopes=["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"])\r\ncreds.refresh(google.auth.transport.requests.Request())\r\n\r\nclient = OpenAI(\r\n base_url="https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/my-startup-dev/locations/global/endpoints/openapi",\r\n api_key=creds.token, # a one-hour token from your login, not a stored key\r\n)\r\nresp = client.chat.completions.create(\r\n model="openai/gpt-oss-120b-maas",\r\n messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}],\r\n)\r\nprint(resp.choices[0].message.content)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e5262890>)])]>

Two things to know:

  • Partner models like Claude need a one-time Enable on their Model Garden card in each project. After that, everyone with access can call them.

  • OpenAI's GPT-6 models arrived in Model Garden on October 21 in private preview for select enterprise customers. When they open up, the same login will work for them too.

Every call lands on one Google Cloud bill, which makes it easier to compare models on cost and quality.

Step three: Give your app its own identity

Your app needs the same thing your developers just got: an identity instead of a key. For a workload, that identity is a service account.

The good news is that the code from Step 2 doesn't change. On your laptop, ADC picks up your own login. On Cloud Run, GKE or Compute Engine, it picks up a short-lived token for the service account attached to the workload, refreshed automatically. So there is nothing in your codebase to leak. A token that escapes is short-lived, usually about an hour, and it only carries the permissions of one service account.

Create the service account and deploy with it:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud iam service-accounts create agent-runtime \\\r\n --display-name="Runtime identity for the app"\r\n\r\ngcloud run deploy my-agent \\\r\n --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/my-startup-prod/agents/api:v1 \\\r\n --service-account=agent-runtime@my-startup-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com \\\r\n --region=us-central1'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e5260890>)])]>

Keep people and production apart. Developers work in my-startup-dev under their own logins, and the app runs in my-startup-prod under its service account. A mistake in one doesn't spend the other's budget.

Step four: Give each identity only what it needs

Removing keys solves the leak problem. The next question is what each identity is allowed to do. If a person or a service account holds the Editor or Owner role, a stolen login or token can still delete resources, change permissions or read data it never needed.

Calling models takes one role, roles/aiplatform.user. The grant looks the same for both kinds of identity.

For people, grant it to a Google group, not to individuals. Onboarding and offboarding then become a group membership change:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-startup-dev \\\r\n --member="group:ai-builders@my-startup.com" \\\r\n --role="roles/aiplatform.user"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e5261510>)])]>

For the app, grant it to the service account:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-startup-prod \\\r\n --member="serviceAccount:agent-runtime@my-startup-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \\\r\n --role="roles/aiplatform.user"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e5263a50>)])]>

It takes about 30 seconds longer than granting Editor. If anything is compromised later, the attacker gets one narrow role instead of the whole project. When someone leaves, remove them from the group and their access ends everywhere at once.

In the Cloud Console, the Grant access dialog has a Help me choose roles button. You describe the task in plain English and Gemini suggests predefined roles. By default the suggestions cover common tasks, which usually means a service's broad Admin, Editor or Viewer role. To get the narrow roles, say so:

What is the narrowest access a service account needs to call Gemini models on Agent Platform?

Three more controls are worth knowing:

  • If your project sits in an organization, the vertexai.allowedModels policy limits which models anyone can call. You list values such as publishers/google/models/gemini-4-hydrogen:predict, and everything else is blocked.

  • The repo includes a one-line audit that lists every service account holding Owner or Editor on a project. Run it now and again before each launch.

  • To stop new keys from being created, enforce Org Policies denying CREATE on apikeys.googleapis.com/Key for API keys and iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation for service account keys.

Step 5: Put the remaining keys in Secret Manager

Some keys won't go away, like Stripe, Slack or your email provider. They belong in Secret Manager, not in .env files, chat threads or the repo. Access works the way it did in Step 4: grant read access on each secret to the identity that needs it.

Test keys go to the developer group:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud secrets create stripe-test-key --data-file=-\r\ngcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding stripe-test-key \\\r\n --member="group:ai-builders@my-startup.com" \\\r\n --role="roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e52623d0>)])]>

Anyone in the group can then fetch the key with their own login:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=stripe-test-key'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e5262c10>)])]>

Live keys stay in the production project, readable only by the app's service account. The app reads them at startup:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'from google.cloud import secretmanager\r\n\r\nsm = secretmanager.SecretManagerServiceClient()\r\nresp = sm.access_secret_version(\r\n name="projects/my-startup-prod/secrets/stripe-live-key/versions/latest"\r\n)\r\nstripe_key = resp.payload.data.decode("utf-8")'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e5263a10>)])]>

Reading --data-file=- from standard input keeps the value out of your shell history. Every read is tied to a named person or service account, and rotating a key means adding one new version. Nothing is redeployed and no file is copied between laptops.

Then finish the job. Go to the AI Studio API keys page and delete every key, personal or shared, that ever left a laptop. A key you have moved away from is still live until you delete it.

What the new setup gives you

Once your people and your app run on identities in a Google Cloud project, several protections become available that a bare key can't offer. You don't need all of them on day one. They are worth knowing about before your first launch.

A spend cap that pauses the service

Standard budget alerts send email while the bill keeps climbing. A spend cap budget, currently in Preview, does more. When estimated spend for one service in one project passes the amount you set, new requests to that service are paused until you lift the cap or the next month starts. Alerts go to billing admins and project owners at 50%, 80% and 100%.

You can create one in the console under Budgets & alerts by choosing Spend cap enforcement, or through the Budget API. The repo wraps the API call and has a dry-run flag so you can inspect the request first:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'python -m bonus_spend_cap.create_spend_cap \\\r\n --billing-account 012345-6789AB-CDEF01 --amount 500 --dry-run'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e5261090>)])]>

Know the limits before relying on it. Each cap covers a single project and a single service. Agent Platform, the Gemini API, Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions are eligible today. Enforcement runs on estimated cost and is not instant. Any overage is billed as normal, so set the number below the amount you can actually afford to lose. A cap also pauses usage covered by commitments, and after you lift it the service can take up to an hour to recover.

Set one cap on the dev project and another on prod. An experiment then can't drain the budget your customers depend on. For a second layer, lower your Agent Platform quotas to what you really need, so a bug or an agent stuck in a loop runs into a ceiling instead of your card limit.

Guardrails on prompts and responses

As soon as real users can type into your app, someone will try to make it ignore its instructions. Model Armor screens prompts and responses for prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, malicious URLs and sensitive data. You create a template once, check each prompt against it and only call the model when it comes back clean. The repo has both halves.

A sandbox for model-written code

If your product lets the model write and run code, for example to analyze a customer's spreadsheet, that code should not run inside your application process. With code execution, the model runs Python in a Google-managed sandbox and hands back the result:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'config=types.GenerateContentConfig(\r\n tools=[types.Tool(code_execution=types.ToolCodeExecution())],\r\n)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f87e5261290>)])]>

The generated code never sees your environment variables, your files or your database.

Someone watching for unusual behavior

Security Command Center surfaces threats and misconfigurations across the project, such as a service account suddenly calling an API it has never used or a workload contacting an unfamiliar host. Together with Cloud Audit Logs, which record who changed what and when, it also gives you the answers your first enterprise customer's security review will ask for. Because every call now comes from a named person or service account, those logs mean something.

Your 20-minute checklist

For your team:

  • Everyone runs gcloud auth application-default login.

  • Grant roles/aiplatform.user to one Google group, and enable the partner models you want.

  • Move shared test keys into Secret Manager, readable by the group.

For your app:

  • Deploy with a service account that holds roles/aiplatform.user and nothing broader.

  • Move live third-party keys into Secret Manager, readable only by that service account.

  • Set a spend cap on each project below the amount you can afford to lose.

For both: Run the key scanner, then delete every AI Studio key at aistudio.google.com/apikey.

None of this slows down building. You keep the speed of the prototype and every model in Model Garden stays one string away. Nobody on the team has to guard a key again. The full code, with a sample for every step and bonus above, is in the companion repo.

Have a scenario you'd like us to cover next? Reach us at Google Cloud for Startups.
